1002.title: Paulinus of Nola (22 June)
1002.hook: a wealthy poet and senator who gave it up to live simply as a bishop
1002.howItsDone: The Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Paulinus of Nola on 22 June; in Nola his memory is tied to a summer festival, and his poems and letters are read by those who study early Christian writing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aloysius Gonzaga, the heir who nursed the sick of Rome. Your line was young and brave.

A letter arrives from an old teacher. It's elegant, a little hurt, and written in verse. Why have you gone quiet? it asks. Why have you left the life we shared, the estates, the books, the clever friends? The student writes back, also in verse. He hasn't stopped writing poetry. He has changed what it's for. Today, a rich man who gave his fortune away and kept his pen. Paulinus of Nola.
screen: `A LETTER IN VERSE.` → `WHY HAVE YOU GONE QUIET?` → `THE ANSWER, ALSO IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: Paulinus belonged to the comfortable old Roman world. He came from a wealthy family in Gaul, studied with the poet Ausonius, held high office, and owned estates. He married a Spanish woman named Therasia. Then their lives turned. Paulinus was baptized, they lost a baby son, and together they decided to give their wealth away. Not in one dramatic gesture, but by selling and giving, steadily, to the poor and to the Church. Jesus had said it to a rich young man. In the Douay-Rheims: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor." In the Gospel that man goes away sad. Paulinus and Therasia did it. Their circle was shocked. Ausonius, his old teacher, wrote asking him to come back. Paulinus answered, in poems, that his heart now belonged to Christ, and that the old gods of poetry no longer had a claim on him. He wasn't giving up beauty. He was turning it toward God. The couple settled at Nola, in southern Italy, beside the tomb of a martyr, Saint Felix, whom Paulinus loved. They lived simply and cared for pilgrims and the poor. Later the people of Nola chose Paulinus as their bishop. He wrote to other Christian writers of his time, including Augustine and Jerome. And each year, for the feast of Felix, he wrote a new poem. So the rich official became a poet bishop: not a man who gave up everything he was, but one who handed it over, his money, his marriage and his craft, and let each one be used for something else.

segments.voice: Let one thing you're grateful for, or one thing you need, come to mind, and find three plain lines for it. Say them silently, then change one word to make them truer. If you pray, let the lines be your prayer today, addressed however you pray; if you don't, keep them as a few honest lines.

1003.title: The Immaculate Heart of Mary
1003.hook: the Saturday after the Sacred Heart, Mary's heart is honored
1003.tomorrow: The first martyrs of Rome (30 June)
1003.howItsDone: The Church keeps the memorial of the Immaculate Heart of Mary on the Saturday after the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart; some Catholics pray the rosary on the day, and some keep a devotion of first Saturdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paulinus of Nola, the rich Roman who gave his wealth away and kept writing. Your line was the poet bishop.

Shepherds crowd in around a manger at night, out of breath, talking over each other. Angels, they say. A sky full of them. Everyone who hears it is amazed. And in the middle of the noise, the young mother says nothing. Luke turns his camera to her face for one sentence, then moves on. On a Friday in the weeks after Pentecost, the Church honors the Sacred Heart of Jesus. The next day, a Saturday, it turns to that quiet face, and the heart behind it. Today, the Immaculate Heart of Mary.
screen: `SHEPHERDS, OUT OF BREATH.` → `EVERYONE AMAZED.` → `THE MOTHER SAYS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Kept, like something put away safely. Pondering, turning it over, the way you turn a stone in your hand. Luke says it again when Jesus is twelve, after he's found in the Temple: his mother kept all these words in her heart. Luke never gives us a speech from Mary at those moments. He gives us her heart, working. A third line is harder. When the baby is presented in the Temple, an old man named Simeon blesses them and says to Mary: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." That's why pictures of the Immaculate Heart often show a heart with a sword through it, or ringed with roses, or burning with flame. Love, and the cost of love, in one picture. The name trips people up. Immaculate means without stain. Catholic teaching holds that Mary was kept free from sin from the first moment of her life; that's the Immaculate Conception, a separate feast in December. This day is about her heart: the inner life of a woman who said yes, kept watch, and stood at the cross. Over time the devotion grew, and some Catholics connect it with the reported apparitions of Mary at Fatima, in Portugal. Not every Christian keeps it. Orthodox Christians honor Mary in their own ways, and some Protestants read these same verses as a picture of faith without a feast for her heart. For Catholics, the two hearts side by side, the Son's on Friday and the mother's on Saturday, say something plain: her heart was pointed toward his.

Hold it with her, quietly. If you pray, entrust her to Mary, whose own heart held so much in silence; if you don't, simply wish her rest and company.

1004.title: The first martyrs of Rome (30 June)
1004.hook: the unnamed Christians killed under Nero
1004.howItsDone: On 30 June the Church keeps an optional memorial of the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church, the day after the Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul; Catholics remember them at Mass and often pray for Christians persecuted today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Immaculate Heart of Mary, who kept the words and pondered them. Your line was her heart.

Rome is burning. For days the fire runs through the city, and when it's out, people want someone to blame. Rumors point at the emperor himself. So Nero points somewhere else: at a small, strange group the city already distrusts, the Christians. What follows is cruel, and public. And almost none of the people who die have names we know. The day before, the Church honors Peter and Paul, names written all over the New Testament. Today it turns to the ones nobody wrote down. Today, the first martyrs of Rome.
screen: `ROME IS BURNING.` → `NERO NEEDS SOMEONE TO BLAME.` → `NAMES NOBODY WROTE DOWN.`

segments.voice: The main account comes not from a Christian but from a Roman historian, Tacitus, who had no sympathy for them and calls their faith a superstition. He records that Nero shifted the blame for the fire onto them, that a great many were arrested, and that they were put to death with mockery: some dressed in animal skins and torn by dogs, some burned as torches when daylight failed. Even Tacitus says the crowd began to feel pity, sensing these people were dying not for the public good but for one man's cruelty. Tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome under Nero too. But this day is for everyone else. Paul had once written to this very church. In the Douay-Rheims he tells them: "your faith is spoken of in the whole world." Some readers wonder how many of the people Paul greets by name at the end of that letter were among those who died. Nobody knows. That's the point of this feast. The Greek word behind martyr means a witness. In Acts, Jesus tells his followers, "you shall be witnesses unto me." A martyr is someone whose death becomes their testimony. These martyrs left none we can read: no last words, no letters, no tombs with names. The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of the faithful as "so great a cloud of witnesses": a crowd, not a list. The Church's calendar has a day for them anyway. They have no names in our books, and the feast rests on the trust that every one of them is known to God.

segments.voice: Think of people who have died for their faith, in any age, whose names never made the news, and of people today who face prison or violence for what they believe, in places you may never see. 1005.title: Thomas (3 July)
1005.hook: the doubter who, tradition says, took the gospel to India
1005.howItsDone: The Church keeps the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle on 3 July; in India, the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala keep it as the feast of the apostle they trace their church to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first martyrs of Rome, a crowd with no names, known to us through Tacitus. Your line was no names, all known.

"Doubting Thomas." People say it at work about the colleague who wants to see the numbers, and at home about the kid who won't believe the stove is hot. It has stuck to him. But in John's Gospel, the first time we hear this man speak, he offers to die. And when he finally believes, what he says about Jesus is startlingly plain. Today, a witness with a nickname he might not have chosen. Thomas.
screen: `DOUBTING THOMAS.` → `THE MAN WHO OFFERED TO DIE.` → `STARTLINGLY PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First scene. Jesus decides to go back toward Judea, where people had tried to stone him, because his friend Lazarus has died. The disciples protest. Thomas, John says, "who is called Didymus," Greek for twin, turns to the others: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Grim, maybe. But brave. Second scene. On the evening of the resurrection day, Jesus appears to the disciples, and Thomas isn't there. They tell him. He refuses to take it secondhand. "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." That's the line that earned the nickname. Third scene, eight days later. Thomas is with them. Jesus comes, stands among them, and offers Thomas exactly what he asked for: put your finger here, see my hands. John never says Thomas touches him. What he says is: "Thomas answered, and said to him: My Lord and my God." Not teacher. Not prophet. Catholics hear in it a full confession of faith in Jesus, from the man who wouldn't believe secondhand. Jesus answers: blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed. Then the Gospel goes quiet about him. Tradition carries on. It says Thomas went east, preached in India, and died there as a martyr. Some Christians in India, above all the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, trace their church to him. Historians debate the details. For those churches, the tradition is their own story.

1006.title: Elizabeth of Portugal (4 July)
1006.hook: a queen who rode between armies to make peace
1006.howItsDone: The Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Elizabeth of Portugal on 4 July; in Portugal, above all in Coimbra where she is buried, she is honored as the Holy Queen, and Catholics ask her prayers for peace in families and between nations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas, the doubter who said my Lord and my God. That was your line.

Two armies face each other across a field. On one side, a king. On the other, his own son, who has risen against him. Banners, horses, men waiting for the signal. And then, tradition says, a woman on a mule rides out alone into the open ground between them. She is the king's wife and the rebel's mother. She stops there and won't move until they talk. Today, the queen in the middle. Elizabeth of Portugal.
screen: `TWO ARMIES ACROSS A FIELD.` → `A FATHER AND HIS SON.` → `A QUEEN RIDES INTO THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Elizabeth was a princess of Aragon, in Spain, married young to King Denis of Portugal. The marriage wasn't easy. Denis was a capable king, and an unfaithful husband. Elizabeth's lives tell of her raising his children by other women alongside her own, and of a quiet, stubborn life of prayer and care for the poor in the middle of a royal court. In public, her work was peace. When her son Afonso rose against his father, the kingdom came close to war between them. Elizabeth went back and forth, pleading with each, and at least once, tradition says, she rode between the two armies to stop the battle before it began. She also helped settle quarrels between Portugal and its neighbors. Jesus says it in the Sermon on the Mount. In the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Notice what a peacemaker in this story actually does. Not a speech from a safe distance. She puts her own body in the gap, loving both sides too much to let either win by killing the other. There's a gentler legend too. Tradition says she was carrying bread to the poor in her cloak when the king stopped her and asked what she had. She opened the cloak, and it was full of roses. The same story is told of another royal Elizabeth, her great-aunt in Hungary, and many readers take it as a picture: charity hidden, and turned to beauty when questioned. After Denis died, Elizabeth gave herself to prayer and service beside the Poor Clares, and tradition says she died while traveling to make peace yet again.

If you pray, hold them both before God; if you don't, keep them both in mind without choosing.

Your line: the peacemaker queen. Sometimes peace needs someone standing right in the middle. Day one thousand six, done.

1007.title: Maria Goretti (6 July)
1007.hook: an eleven-year-old who forgave the young man who killed her; he later repented
1007.tomorrow: Our Lady of Mount Carmel (16 July)
1007.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Maria Goretti on 6 July, and some parishes remember victims of violence in the prayers at Mass that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Elizabeth of Portugal, the queen who rode out between armies. Your line was the peacemaker queen.

A farmhouse in the Italian countryside, shared by two poor families. In one, a widow and her children; the oldest girl, Maria, minds the little ones while her mother works the fields. In the other, a young man named Alessandro. One afternoon, when the house is nearly empty, he tries to force himself on her. She refuses him, and he stabs her. She is carried to a hospital, and she does not live long. This is a hard story, and the Church tells it gently. It doesn't dwell on the attack. It turns to something she said before she died.
screen: `TWO FAMILIES, ONE FARMHOUSE.` → `SHE REFUSES HIM.` → `WHAT SHE SAID BEFORE SHE DIED.`

segments.voice: The Church's account says Maria Goretti was eleven. As she lay dying, she was asked about the young man who had hurt her, and the account says she forgave him and hoped to see him in heaven. That's the whole of her teaching, one sentence from a child. Catholics hear in it an echo of the cross. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says from the cross: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Then the story turns to Alessandro. He goes to prison, and for a long time, by the account, he shows no sorrow at all. Then, tradition says, he sees Maria in a dream, offering him flowers. Something in him breaks open. Years later, out of prison, he goes to Maria's mother and asks her forgiveness. She gives it. The story told about that day says the two of them went to Mass together and received communion side by side. Afterward Alessandro lived out his life quietly among Capuchin friars, working as a gardener and a porter. Catholics honor Maria as a martyr, and her feast is kept on the sixth of July. One thing matters here. Her forgiveness was her gift, freely given. It isn't a rule laid on anyone who has been hurt, and it doesn't erase what was done. Catholic writers have said this carefully: forgiving is not pretending, and it never asks someone to stay in danger. What her story holds out is something else: a wound that, in time, became a door for the person who caused it.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE FROM A CHILD.` · `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` · `A DREAM, A PRISON, A MOTHER.` · `A GIFT, NOT A RULE.` · then, large: `FORGIVENESS AT ELEVEN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind people hurt by violence, near or far: a name from the news, a street in your own town, someone you know who never talks about it. Don't push for feelings; just keep them company for a while. If you pray, pray for them, or say the Our Father slowly with them in mind; if you don't, hold them in your attention, one breath for each.
Maria Goretti. A young Italian girl who refused her attacker, forgave him before she died, and whose forgiveness reached him years later.
Your line: forgiveness at eleven. Her forgiveness was hers to give, and it reached further than anyone expected. Day one thousand seven.

1008.title: Our Lady of Mount Carmel (16 July)
1008.hook: the Carmelites' feast, with the brown scapular as a sign of belonging
1008.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of Mount Carmel on 16 July, and some receive the brown scapular from a priest and wear it afterward under their clothes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maria Goretti, whose forgiveness reached the man who hurt her. Your line was forgiveness at eleven.

Two small squares of brown wool, joined by two thin cords. That's the whole object. One square rests on the chest, the other between the shoulder blades, and the cords lie over the shoulders, usually hidden under a shirt. You could stand next to someone wearing one all day and never know. Some Catholics wear one from childhood on. Today it comes out from under the shirt, on the feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, the title the Carmelites gave to Mary.
screen: `TWO SQUARES OF BROWN WOOL.` → `ONE FRONT, ONE BACK.` → `HIDDEN UNDER A SHIRT.`

segments.voice: Start with the mountain. Mount Carmel stands above the sea in the Holy Land, and in the books of Kings it's where Elijah calls down fire, then prays for rain until a small cloud rises from the sea. Tradition says that, much later, Christian hermits went to live on that mountain, close to Elijah's memory, and built a chapel to Mary. They became the Carmelites, and Mary under the title of Mount Carmel became their patron. Now the word. A scapular began as part of a monk's or friar's habit: a long strip of cloth worn over the shoulders, hanging down in front and behind, like an apron worn both ways. Some explain it as a sign of taking on a yoke. The brown scapular is that habit shrunk to two small pieces of cloth, so people who aren't friars or nuns can wear a piece of the Carmelite habit too. Tradition says Mary gave the scapular to a Carmelite named Simon Stock, with a promise of her protection. That's where the line comes from: under her mantle. A mantle is a cloak, and the old picture is Mary spreading hers over the people she protects. Here the Church is careful. It calls the scapular a sacramental. Not a charm, not a ticket, but a sign of belonging and a reminder to live like it, to pray and to trust Mary's care. The cloth does nothing by itself. The life under it is the point.
screen: `ELIJAH'S MOUNTAIN.` · `A STRIP OF CLOTH OVER THE SHOULDERS.` · `THE HABIT, MADE SMALL.` · `A SIGN, NOT A CHARM.` · then, large: `UNDER HER MANTLE.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop and notice what rests there: the collar and the straps, and the jobs, worries and people you carry today. Picture a cloak laid over all of it, not taking it away, just covering it. If you pray, ask Mary to keep you under her mantle; if you don't, let your shoulders be held by the chair and the air.
